reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A common cause of persistent or recurrent glomerular (dysmorphic) microscopic haematuria, frequently found in several family members
Often caused by heterozygous mutations in the COL4A3 or COL4A4 genes encoding type IV collagen, the same collagen family affected in Alport syndrome
The hallmark on electron microscopy is diffuse, uniform thinning of the glomerular basement membrane
Most patients have isolated haematuria with normal or only minimal proteinuria, normal blood pressure, and preserved kidney function
Unlike Alport syndrome, it is not typically associated with sensorineural hearing loss or ocular abnormalities
It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion once IgA nephropathy, Alport syndrome, and urological causes have been considered
Biopsy is not always required; the diagnosis is often based on the clinical picture and family history of benign haematuria
Management is usually limited to reassurance and periodic monitoring of blood pressure, proteinuria, and kidney function
reference.pathophysiology: Thin basement membrane nephropathy is a hereditary disorder of the glomerular basement membrane, commonly due to heterozygous mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4. These genes encode alpha chains of type IV collagen that form the structural scaffold of the basement membrane; the mutations produce a thin but generally intact membrane. The attenuated barrier allows red cells to escape into the urinary space, causing glomerular haematuria, yet the membrane usually retains enough integrity to preserve filtration and limit protein loss. Because the same collagen genes underlie Alport syndrome, TBMN can be viewed as part of a spectrum of type IV collagen disease, and a minority of carriers may show a more progressive course.
additionalDifferentials: Urological causes of haematuria (stones, tumours, infection)
additionalInvestigations: Urine microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
Quantification of proteinuria and monitoring of kidney function
Kidney biopsy with electron microscopy in selected cases, and genetic testing for COL4A3/COL4A4 where appropriate
redFlags: Development of significant or rising proteinuria
New hypertension or declining kidney function
Hearing loss or ocular findings suggesting Alport syndrome instead
reference.prognosis: The great majority of patients have a benign course with lifelong isolated haematuria and stable kidney function, although a subset with underlying collagen IV mutations may progress and warrants ongoing surveillance.
pitfalls: Labelling haematuria as benign without excluding Alport syndrome, especially when proteinuria or family kidney failure is present
Missing the overlap with type IV collagen disease and its potential for progression
Failing to check for proteinuria and hypertension on follow-up
Overlooking coexisting IgA nephropathy in a patient with thin membranes
management: Reassurance without specific drug therapy for the typical case of isolated microscopic haematuria with preserved renal function
Institute renoprotection with a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor (ACE inhibitor or ARB) if proteinuria or hypertension develops
Monitor periodically with blood pressure, quantification of proteinuria and renal function to detect the minority who progress
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and manage cardiovascular risk factors
Screen family members for haematuria and offer genetic testing for COL4A3/COL4A4 variants, given overlap with the Alport spectrum
Refer to nephrology for atypical features — significant proteinuria, declining function, or hearing or ocular signs suggesting Alport syndrome
